working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: A no-nonsense decision guide that helps regular UK walkers work out which type of trolley suits their specific situation, rather than defaulting to 'electric is better'. The post leans into real UK-specific variables: hilly heathland versus flat links, small car boots, winter mud, and the cost gap between entry-level electric and a decent push trolley.
research_notes:
- Two dominant market types: push (manual 3-wheel) and electric (manual-steer, remote, or follow). Pull trolleys (2-wheel, dragged behind) are considered outdated and harder on the body.
- Push trolleys are lighter, cheaper, fold more compactly, and typically offer more onboard storage than electric equivalents.
- Electric trolleys are heavier due to motor and battery, but the effort to push the weight is removed, which conserves energy over a round, particularly on hilly courses.
- Key electric sub-types: manual-steer electric (you walk behind and steer), remote-controlled (steer from a distance), follow (trolley tracks you autonomously). Follow models are the most expensive tier.
- PowaKaddy and Motocaddy are the two dominant brands in the UK electric market.
- Example electric price points (from published guides, accurate at time of search): entry-level electric (e.g. Motocaddy SE) around £499; mid-range compact electric (e.g. PowaKaddy FX1 36-hole) around £549; GPS+DHC models (e.g. Motocaddy M5 GPS DHC) around £1,099.
- Example push trolley price points: PowaKaddy Micra £189; Clicgear 4.0 £219. Stewart R1-S sits at a premium push-trolley price point.
- Battery sizing matters: 18-hole lithium covers a standard round; 27- or 36-hole batteries suit hillier courses or back-to-back days.
- Electronic Braking Systems (EBS / DHC on Motocaddy) automatically slow the trolley on downhill slopes. Relevant for steep UK parkland and heathland courses.
- Lithium batteries are lighter and longer-lasting than older lead-acid types.
- Fold size is important for small car boots. Some electric trolleys fold very compactly; push trolleys generally fold smaller and lighter.
- Electric trolleys heavier to lift in/out of boot even if they fold well.
- For flat or shorter courses, a push trolley may be entirely sufficient.
- Three-wheel push design preferred over two-wheel pull for body mechanics (pushing weight forward vs twisting arm behind).
- UK-specific angle: hilly inland parkland and heathland courses favour electric; flat coastal links courses less demanding on push users.
- Note: prices cited are from published buying guides and may change. Do not present as current guaranteed prices; use as general illustration of price tier relationships only.
